profiles.summary: Mainnet still runs release v0.16.5 with revision MONAD_TEN. The one new opcode level fact is how the client treats a call to an account whose EIP-7702 delegation points at a Monad precompile: the call fails, where Ethereum would run empty code.

deltas.delta: A call to an account with code 0xef0100 followed by the staking address 0x1000 or the reserve balance address 0x1001 fails with empty return data for every calldata, with and without value. The same account pointed at ecrecover, sha256, identity or P256 returns success with no data, as on Ethereum. The client sets the Delegated flag on such a message (runtime/call.cpp lines 41 to 56 and 108 to 175) and check_call_monad_precompile rejects any message whose flags are not zero (monad_precompiles.cpp lines 43 to 49). A native take to such an account reverts at src/types/Currency.sol:51-53, so the difference is fail closed.

profiles.summary: The files of mega-evm that decide call interception, deposit accounting, block limits, precompiles and storage gas are byte identical at tag v1.7.3 and on the main branch. Interception depends on the target address of a call, so DELEGATECALL and CALLCODE never reach a system contract's native behaviour.

deltas.delta: The four interceptors compare call_inputs.target_address with the system contract address (system/intercept.rs lines 301, 430 and 497). Under DELEGATECALL and CALLCODE the target address is the calling account, so the call runs the Solidity code of the system contract in the caller's context. On chain, DELEGATECALL and CALLCODE of disableVolatileDataAccess, enableVolatileDataAccess, isVolatileDataAccessDisabled and remainingComputeGas revert with NotIntercepted (0x1894f076), while CALL and STATICCALL are intercepted, the STATICCALL of disableVolatileDataAccess included.

deltas.delta: The switch set by disableVolatileDataAccess ends when the frame that set it returns. A frame at the PoolManager address called a second contract that disabled access, saw isVolatileDataAccessDisabled true and a TIMESTAMP reader revert, and returned. The first frame then read isVolatileDataAccessDisabled false and the TIMESTAMP reader succeeded. A hook, a token or a payout recipient therefore cannot leave the switch on for the rest of the PoolManager call.

profiles.summary: The public gateway streams mini-blocks and no pending transactions. Inside an EVM block the order is the order of the 10 millisecond mini-blocks, and a higher priority fee does not come first even inside one mini-block. A deposit whose sender account is empty counts as one new state entry even when it fails the intrinsic gas test.

deltas.delta: A subscription to newPendingTransactions on the public WebSocket gateway delivered no notification in 214 seconds, during which the miniBlocks subscription delivered 21,400 consecutive mini-blocks with 5,566 transactions. The pool of the sequencer cannot be observed from public data, and the FAQ says that there is no way to check its contents.
deltas.source: wss://mainnet.megaeth.com/ws eth_subscribe newPendingTransactions and miniBlocks, 214 seconds from EVM block 32,658,901 on 2026-11-23 and https://docs.megaeth.com/developer-docs/faq.md

deltas.delta: 213 fully captured EVM blocks hold 99 or 100 mini-blocks each. The median mini-block interval is 10.06 ms and consecutive EVM blocks start 0.999 to 1.001 s apart. Among 149 mini-blocks with two or more user transactions, 44 of 324 neighbouring pairs from different senders have the later one paying the higher priority fee. Across mini-blocks of one EVM block the count is 597 of 2,645. The sequencer signs each mini-block header, and the mini-block page says it executes transactions continuously and seals what it executed every 10 ms.

deltas.delta: For a deposit whose sender account is empty the handler records one new account on the state growth counter (evm/execution.rs lines 883 to 918) before the final test of intrinsic gas against the gas limit (lines 921 to 941). A deposit that fails that test becomes a failed deposit through catch_error, and execute_transaction then reads the usage of the limiter (evm/mod.rs lines 382 to 391), which is reset only when the next transaction starts. The entry is counted.

profiles.summary: The OptimismPortal of MegaETH rejects a deposit with more than 1,000,000 gas, where OP Mainnet and Base accept 5,000,000. Storage gas for a first write to a slot scales with the size of the SALT bucket that holds the slot, and any account can grow a chosen bucket. Real liquidity removals use 183,000 to 314,000 gas, so the margin under the cap is about 700,000 gas.

deltas.delta: depositTransaction on the MegaETH portal 0x7f82f57F0Dd546519324392e408b01fcC7D709e8 (implementation 0x55400445e384393f9c1be23e7e734e8d44ed9fd9, version 3.15.2) succeeds in simulation for a gas limit of 21,000, 60,000, 999,999 and 1,000,000 and reverts with 'L2 message gas must not exceed 1 million' for 1,000,001, 2,000,000, 19,000,000 and 30,000,000. The same call with 5,000,000 succeeds on the OP Mainnet and Base portals. The implementation bytecode also holds the string 'MEGA_SYSTEM_ADDRESS cannot create deposit transactions'. The two force inclusion pages of the documentation do not mention the cap. resourceConfig() still reports 20,000,000 gas of deposits per L1 block.

Only system originated transactions are charged at multiplier 1. The source states that a user deposit is never matched by that test (system/tx.rs lines 115 to 137, external/gas.rs, functions sstore_set_gas and load_bucket_cost_multiplier).

deltas.delta: SALT has 16,777,216 buckets of which 65,536 hold metadata, so 16,711,680 hold data. The bucket of an entry is a hash with four fixed public seeds over the address and slot, modulo that number. On insertion a bucket whose used count exceeds 80 percent of capacity is rehashed to a capacity doubled until the count fits. The README says expansion is automatic and contraction is manual.

findings.title: A forced transaction from L1 may carry at most 1,000,000 gas on MegaETH, and any account can raise the storage gas of a chosen PoolManager slot above that for about 0.003 ETH, which closes the L1 exit of the position that must write the slot
findings.difference: Ethereum prices a storage write the same for every slot, and a standard OP Stack portal sells up to 20,000,000 gas to one deposit. MegaETH charges storage gas for a first write to a slot in proportion to the size of the SALT bucket that holds the slot, lets anyone grow a bucket by writing other entries into it, and runs a portal that rejects a deposit with more than 1,000,000 gas.
findings.mechanism: 1. The only way to act on MegaETH without the sequencer is depositTransaction on the L1 portal. In simulation at L1 block 26,479,461 the portal accepts a gas limit of 1,000,000 and reverts with 'L2 message gas must not exceed 1 million' for 1,000,001 and above. The OP Mainnet and Base portals accept 5,000,000. 2. A user deposit pays the same storage gas as any user transaction: 20,000 times (multiplier minus 1) for a zero to nonzero SSTORE, with multiplier equal to the capacity of the slot's bucket divided by 256, read from the parent block. Only system originated transactions are exempt. 3. A bucket doubles whenever its used count exceeds 80 percent of its capacity. The bucket of an entry is a hash with public fixed seeds over address and slot, modulo 16,711,680, so an account that wants entries in one bucket tries about 16.7 million slot numbers of its own contract per entry off chain. A transaction may add 1,000 new entries, and each is priced at the multiplier of the parent block. Seven transactions in seven blocks with 1,000 entries each take a bucket from multiplier 1 to 8, 16, 16, 32, 32, 32 and 64 and cost 22.6, 163, 323, 323, 643, 643 and 643 million gas, 2.76 billion in total, which is 0.0028 ETH at the base fee of 1,000,000 wei. 6,554 entries are the minimum. 4. At multiplier 64 one first write to a slot in that bucket costs 1,260,000 storage gas, which is more than a deposit can carry. Two such writes at multiplier 32 cost 1,240,000 on top of a removal that uses 183,000 to 314,000 gas. 5. Every liquidity change runs Position.update, which stores the current fee growth inside the range in two slots without any condition (src/libraries/Position.sol:99-100). A position whose two ticks it initialized itself starts with zero in both, because getFeeGrowthInside returns the global value minus the value just copied into the lower tick (src/libraries/Pool.sol:488-511, 533-539). Once swaps have paid fees in the range, the next update of that position is a zero to nonzero write to one or two slots whose numbers follow from the pool id, the owner, the ticks and the salt, all public in the ModifyLiquidity log (src/PoolManager.sol:175). 6. At block 32,659,841 the PoolManager has 137 positions with liquidity. 36 need such a write for their next update and 29 of them need two. 7. An account that has grown the buckets of those slots has made the removal of that position cost more than 1,000,000 gas for good, since nothing I found shrinks a bucket without the operator. Through the sequencer the same removal costs about 0.0000013 ETH more and still works. Through the portal it cannot be sent. No bucket above minimum size was observed on mainnet, and I could not read bucket capacities over the public endpoint, so steps 3 and 4 rest on the specification and the client and SALT sources and were not replayed on chain.
findings.impact: A liquidity provider whose position was prepared this way can leave only through the sequencer. If the sequencer refuses the provider's transactions or is down, the L1 route that F-017 relies on does not exist for that position, and the position stays in the pool and open to swaps for as long as that lasts. Preparing one slot of each of the 36 positions that are exposed today costs about 0.1 ETH. The MegaETH PoolManager holds about 17,000 dollars. Swaps and removals that write no zero slot are not affected.
findings.preconditions: The position must store a zero fee growth for a currency in which fees have accrued since. Any account can do the preparation: it spends about 0.003 ETH per slot at any time before the provider tries to leave. The freeze itself then needs the sequencer to keep the provider's transactions out, which is why the actor is recorded as operator. The other way to keep them out is a pool that stays full of earlier transactions as described in F-062, whose ordering assumption is not confirmed.
findings.mitigations: A provider can touch a position once through the sequencer after fees have accrued in both currencies, for example by collecting fees, so that both slots hold nonzero values and later updates pay no storage gas for them. A provider can take proceeds as native ETH or to an address that already holds the token, since a first token balance is also a zero to nonzero write. The operator can raise the portal cap, charge user deposits at multiplier 1 as it does for system transactions, or shrink grown buckets.

findings.title: MegaETH orders transactions by time in 10 millisecond mini-blocks and skips every candidate once a block has 1,000 new state entries, so a queue of filling transactions delays later ones by its length if skipped transactions keep their place
findings.difference: MegaETH skips every candidate transaction of a block once the block has reached 1,000 new state entries, executes transactions as they arrive and commits to their order every 10 ms. Ethereum has no per block cap on new state and orders by fee.
findings.mechanism: 1. Unchanged from cycle 4 and confirmed there: pre_execution_check rejects every candidate once the block's state growth counter has reached 1,000, the transaction that reaches the limit is included, and one transaction may create 1,000 entries for 22,559,525 gas, about 0.0000226 ETH. 2. New: the order inside a block is the order of mini-blocks. In a capture of 21,400 consecutive mini-blocks, 213 EVM blocks hold 99 or 100 mini-blocks each at a median spacing of 10.06 ms, and each mini-block header is signed by the sequencer, so a transaction cannot be placed ahead of one that was already streamed. Inside a mini-block the order does not follow the fee either: 44 of 324 neighbouring pairs from different senders have the later one paying more. A user cannot buy a place ahead of a filling transaction. 3. Still not confirmed: what the pool does with transactions that were skipped. The executor comment says a rejected transaction is typically put back in the pool, the specification says it may be reconsidered in a later block, and neither states its place. The public gateway accepts a subscription to pending transactions and delivers none, so arrival times cannot be compared with inclusion order from public data, and no block with a full state budget was found to observe. If skipped transactions stay ahead of later arrivals, N filling transactions queued from several accounts close N consecutive one second blocks for everything that arrived after them, at about 0.0000226 ETH per second, 1.95 ETH per day. The documentation allows 500 pending transactions per account. 4. Correction to step 6 of the cycle 4 text: the L1 route does not offer 20,000,000 gas to one transaction. The portal rejects a deposit above 1,000,000 gas, and resourceConfig allows 20,000,000 gas of deposits per L1 block in total. A removal through the PositionManager uses 183,000 to 314,000 gas and fits. The deposits of one L1 block still cannot fill the state budget before the last of them runs: a deposit from an empty sender counts as one entry even when it fails for lack of intrinsic gas, the portal's minimum gas limit is 21,000, and 20,000,000 divided by 21,000 is 952. 5. The L1 route is closed for a position whose fee growth slots sit in a SALT bucket that someone has grown, as the first finding of this file describes. For such a position the delay cannot be bypassed.
findings.impact: No funds are lost. Every user of the chain, liquidity providers included, waits as long as the sender keeps a queue and pays for it. A user can leave through an L1 deposit of at most 1,000,000 gas, which costs L1 gas and lands within minutes, unless the position was prepared as in the first finding.
findings.preconditions: The sender funds several accounts and pays about 0.0000226 ETH per second of delay. The pool keeps skipped transactions ahead of later arrivals, which is the unconfirmed link. The sequencer does not filter the sender.
findings.mitigations: Integrators who must exit under load can send the exit as an L1 deposit with a gas limit of at most 1,000,000. Providers can keep their fee growth slots nonzero as described in the first finding. The operator can filter or reorder pool entries with large state growth.

leadResults.answer: First half answered: the order inside a block is the order of the 10 ms mini-blocks, and the fee does not order transactions even inside one mini-block (44 of 324 neighbouring pairs from different senders have the later one paying more, in 21,400 consecutive mini-blocks). Second half still open: the public gateway delivered no pending transaction in 214 seconds, the FAQ says the pool cannot be inspected, and the only text on skipped transactions is an executor comment that they are typically put back in the pool. Their place there is unknown.

Not observed and not excluded. Under the time order shown above a run of N filling transactions would hold N blocks if skipped transactions keep their place, at 0.0000226 ETH per block. The only documented pool limit remains 500 pending transactions per account. New for the way out: a forced transaction from L1 is limited to 1,000,000 gas, a normal removal fits, and the route can be closed per position by growing a SALT bucket (first finding of this file).

No example in either direction. A counterexample cannot pass validation: block/executor.rs applies pre_execution_check to every transaction, and the stateless validator pins the same code at v1.7.3, so a block with a transaction after the limit was reached is invalid. A positive example needs a transaction near 1,000 new entries, and block gas does not find one: a scan of gasUsedRatio by eth_feeHistory over about 4.4 million blocks between 2,000,000 and 28,114,829 found 13,609 blocks at or above 22.5 million gas, far too many to trace, and the scan was stopped because the endpoint slowed to one batch per minute. An index of state growth per transaction would be needed.

Monad only. 1,438 xStocks tokens are pool currencies, none has a multiplier change pending at block 124,780,980, the PoolManager holds at most 12,953 base units of any of them and held 0 SNDKx around the activation block 123,831,381. The balance above what pools record is 7 base units of SNDKx. The other chains of this lead belong to other units.

The comparison of first seen times with mini-block order cannot be made from public data: the pending transaction subscription of the public gateway is silent. The mini-block capture shows time order and no fee order. The deposit question is answered: a deposit from an empty sender that fails the intrinsic gas test still counts as one new state entry, and at most 952 such deposits fit in one L1 block, so the margin of 48 entries stands.

Monad only. As for L-293, and for the wrappers: 1,267 wrappers of xStocks tokens are pool currencies, 13 have a PoolManager balance, every wrapper converts one unit into exactly the multiplier of its underlying token, and wSNDKx has no supply. No SNDKx pool on Monad held liquidity at timestamp 1,795,167,000, so there were no swaps against stale liquidity to read.

Cost to raise one bucket, at the base fee of 1,000,000 wei and 1,000 new entries per block priced at the parent multiplier: multiplier 2 and 8 need one block and 22.6 million gas (205 entries suffice for 2), 16 needs 2 blocks and 185 million gas, 64 needs 7 blocks and 2.76 billion gas (0.0028 ETH), 128 needs 14 blocks and 11.7 billion gas (0.012 ETH), 1,024 needs at least 105 blocks and 711 billion gas (0.71 ETH), in transactions of fewer than 1,000 entries near the end because 1,000 writes at multiplier 512 exceed the gas limit of 10 billion. Entries for a chosen bucket need no cleverness: the hash seeds are public and one hit takes about 16.7 million trials off chain. Zero to nonzero writes: in a removal the two fee growth slots of the position when they hold zero and fees have accrued (36 of 137 live positions), plus the recipient's token balance slot in the token; in a claim mint the balance slot of a first claim; in a take the recipient's token balance slot, or account creation for a native payout to an empty account. The clearance of cycles 1 and 2 used a forced inclusion budget of 20,000,000 gas. The portal allows 1,000,000 per transaction, so multiplier 64 on one slot already closes the L1 route. This is the first finding of this file.
